courseTitle: AI Content & Copywriting VA: From Zero to First Client
courseDescription: A complete beginner-to-job-ready training program for aspiring AI Content & Copywriting Virtual Assistants. Covers AI writing and design tools, brand voice, social captions, blog and SEO content, email and sales copy, portfolio-building, resume and proposal writing, and how to land and manage your first content client.
priceNote: One-time payment unlocks lifetime access to all modules, video lessons, quizzes, and your Certificate of Completion.

modules.title: Module 1: Starting Out as an AI Content & Copywriting VA

lessons.title: What Is an AI Content & Copywriting VA?

slides.heading: What Is an AI Content & Copywriting VA?
bullets: Welcome to your AI Content VA journey
Uses AI tools to produce content and copy faster
A specialist within the broader AI-Powered VA world
slides.narration: Welcome to Module 1 of your AI Content & Copywriting VA training. An AI Content & Copywriting VA uses tools like ChatGPT, Jasper, and Canva AI to produce social captions, blog posts, emails, and marketing copy faster and more consistently, while still applying real editing skill and brand judgment.

slides.heading: What an AI Content VA Actually Does Day to Day
bullets: Drafts a batch of social captions or blog posts with AI
Edits and polishes drafts to match a client's brand voice
Plans and organizes a content calendar around AI-assisted work
slides.narration: On a typical day, an AI Content VA might draft a week's worth of social captions using AI, edit and polish them until they genuinely sound like the client's brand, and organize everything into a simple content calendar so nothing gets missed.

slides.heading: Why Businesses Hire a Dedicated AI Content Specialist
bullets: Anyone can generate a draft - matching brand voice is the hard part
Volume content needs a consistent editing process
Business owners want content that doesn't sound generic
slides.narration: Anyone can type a prompt into ChatGPT, but making the result consistently sound like a specific brand, week after week, at real volume, is genuinely difficult - business owners hire a dedicated Content VA so their content never sounds like generic AI filler.

slides.heading: Is This Niche Right for You?
bullets: You enjoy writing and editing
You're good at noticing tone and word choice
You like organizing a steady content workflow
slides.narration: This niche is a great fit if you genuinely enjoy writing and editing, if you naturally notice small differences in tone and word choice, and if you like the structure of running a steady, organized content workflow for a client.

lessons.title: Skills and Traits of a Great AI Content VA

slides.heading: Core Skills You'll Build
bullets: Prompting AI for on-brand first drafts
Editing AI output until it sounds genuinely human
Planning content around client goals, not just filling a calendar
slides.narration: Over this training, you'll build three core skills: prompting AI tools to produce a strong on-brand first draft, editing that draft until it sounds genuinely human and specific to the client, and planning content that actually serves the client's real goals rather than just filling a calendar.

slides.heading: Traits Clients Look For
bullets: A sharp eye for anything that sounds 'too AI'
Reliability - content goes out on schedule
Genuine curiosity about the client's business and audience
slides.narration: Clients trust AI Content VAs who can immediately spot phrasing that sounds generically AI-generated, who reliably deliver content on schedule, and who take genuine interest in understanding the client's business and audience rather than treating every client the same.

slides.heading: A Day in the Life
bullets: Morning: review yesterday's AI drafts with fresh eyes
Midday: research, prompt, and draft new content
End of day: schedule finished content and plan tomorrow
slides.narration: A typical day might start with a fresh-eyes review of yesterday's AI drafts, move into researching a topic and drafting new content with AI assistance, and end with scheduling finished pieces and planning what's next on the calendar.

slides.heading: Where Growth Leads
bullets: Move from single posts into full content strategy
Specialize in high-value formats like email or SEO
Manage several clients' content calendars at once
slides.narration: As you gain experience, you can grow from writing individual posts into shaping a client's full content strategy, specialize in high-value formats like email marketing or SEO content, and eventually manage several clients' content calendars for a full-time income.

lessons.title: Understanding Brand Voice in the Age of AI

slides.heading: Why Brand Voice Matters More With AI, Not Less
bullets: AI defaults to a generic, polished tone
Without direction, everything starts sounding the same
Your job is steering it back to THEIR specific voice
slides.narration: Left on its own, AI tends to default to a smooth, generic, slightly corporate tone - which means without deliberate direction, a client's content can start sounding just like every other business using the same tools. Your job is steering every draft back to their specific, distinct voice.

slides.heading: Building a Brand Voice Profile for AI Prompts
bullets: 3-5 words that describe the tone
Real example sentences the client already loved
Words and phrases to avoid entirely
slides.narration: Build a simple brand voice profile for every client: three to five words describing their tone, several real example sentences they've already loved, and a short list of words or phrases they specifically want to avoid - feed this into every prompt you write.

slides.heading: Questions to Ask a New Client About Voice
bullets: Who is your ideal customer, exactly?
What tone do you want - playful, formal, warm?
Show me a piece of content you loved, and one you hated
slides.narration: Before writing anything, ask who their ideal customer is exactly, what tone they want their brand to have, and ask them to show you one piece of content they loved and one they disliked - real examples teach you more than any description.

slides.heading: Staying Aligned Over Time
bullets: Check in regularly, don't assume voice stays static
Ask for feedback on your first few AI-assisted pieces
Update your brand voice profile as things evolve
slides.narration: Brand voice can shift over time, so check in with your client regularly, especially in the first few weeks, and don't be afraid to ask directly whether a piece landed the way they wanted - then update your saved brand voice profile accordingly.

lessons.title: Setting Up Your AI Content Workspace & Tools Checklist

slides.heading: What You Actually Need to Get Started
bullets: A laptop or desktop with a modern browser
Free accounts on ChatGPT/Claude and Canva to start
A simple document for saving brand voice profiles
slides.narration: You don't need expensive software to start - a reliable computer, free accounts on ChatGPT or Claude and Canva, and a simple shared document for saving each client's brand voice profile is enough to begin practicing.

slides.heading: Organizing Your Content Workflow
bullets: One folder per client for drafts and assets
A simple content calendar - date, platform, status
A running prompt library for content types you write often
slides.narration: Keep each client's drafts and brand assets in their own folder, track everything on a simple content calendar with date, platform, and status columns, and build a running library of prompts that consistently work well for the content types you write most often.

slides.heading: Understanding Free vs Paid AI Content Tools
bullets: Free tiers are enough to learn and practice
Paid tiers unlock higher volume and better models
Decide per client who pays for premium tools
slides.narration: Free tiers of most AI content tools are genuinely enough to learn on and even complete simple client tasks, while paid tiers unlock higher usage volume and smarter models - always clarify with each client upfront whether you or they cover any tool subscription cost.

slides.heading: Ready for Module 2
bullets: You know what the role involves
You understand why brand voice matters
Next: the specific AI content tools you'll use daily
slides.narration: You now understand what an AI Content & Copywriting VA does and why brand voice matters more than ever. In Module 2, we'll get hands-on with the specific tools you'll use every day on the job.

modules.title: Module 2: Essential AI Content Tools Every Content VA Must Know

lessons.title: ChatGPT and Claude for Long-Form and Short-Form Writing

slides.heading: Why These Two Tools First
bullets: Strong general-purpose writers for almost any format
Handle both short captions and long articles well
Most clients have already heard of at least one
slides.narration: ChatGPT and Claude are both strong general-purpose writers capable of handling anything from a one-line caption to a full long-form article, and learning these two tools well covers the large majority of everyday content-writing tasks.

slides.heading: Prompting for Short-Form Content
bullets: Give the platform, the goal, and the exact tone
Ask for several variations to choose from
Iterate on the best one rather than starting over
slides.narration: For short-form content like captions, specify the exact platform, the post's goal, and the tone you want, and ask for three or four variations rather than just one - then iterate on whichever version is closest rather than starting from scratch.

slides.heading: Prompting for Long-Form Content
bullets: Give an outline first, then draft section by section
Feed in research or source material directly
Long pieces benefit from more back-and-forth refinement
slides.narration: For longer content, it often works best to have the AI draft an outline first, then expand each section individually while feeding in any relevant research - long-form pieces generally benefit from more rounds of refinement than a quick caption does.

slides.heading: Keeping Long-Form Content From Feeling Repetitive
bullets: AI can repeat the same phrases across a long piece
Ask it to vary sentence structure and vocabulary
Read the full piece aloud before calling it done
slides.narration: AI-generated long-form content can fall into repeating certain phrases or sentence structures - explicitly ask for variety, and always read the finished piece aloud before calling it done, since repetition is much easier to hear than to spot by eye.

lessons.title: Jasper and Copy.ai for Marketing Copy at Scale

slides.heading: Why Use a Dedicated Marketing Copy Tool
bullets: Built-in templates for ads, landing pages, and emails
Faster than prompting from scratch every time
Worth it once volume gets high enough
slides.narration: Jasper and Copy.ai come with built-in templates specifically for ads, landing pages, product descriptions, and emails - for a client needing a high volume of marketing copy every month, these purpose-built templates are often faster than prompting from scratch each time.

slides.heading: Using Templates Without Sounding Templated
bullets: Templates are a starting structure, not a final answer
Always personalize with real client details
Edit out anything that feels like stock marketing language
slides.narration: Treat a template as a starting structure rather than a finished answer - always personalize it with real client-specific details, and edit out any phrasing that feels like generic, interchangeable stock marketing language.

slides.heading: When a Dedicated Tool Is (and Isn't) Worth It
bullets: High-volume, template-friendly content: often worth it
Highly custom, brand-specific storytelling: ChatGPT/Claude may do better
Consider the client's budget for extra tool subscriptions
slides.narration: A dedicated tool like Jasper tends to earn its cost for high-volume, template-friendly content like ad variations, but for highly custom brand storytelling, a general tool like ChatGPT or Claude with a strong brand voice prompt may actually perform better.

slides.heading: Building a Repeatable System With Templates
bullets: Save your best-performing template setups
Reuse the same structure for similar future requests
Track which templates actually convert for clients
slides.narration: Once you find a template setup that performs well for a client, save it and reuse that same structure for similar future requests - and where possible, track which templates actually drive real results so you know what to keep using.

lessons.title: Canva AI and Design-Integrated Content Creation

slides.heading: Why Canva AI Fits This Role Well
bullets: Combines writing help directly with visual design
Magic Write drafts text right inside your design
No separate design skill required
slides.narration: Canva's built-in AI features, including Magic Write, let you draft text directly inside the same tool you're using to design the visual - meaning captions, headlines, and graphics can all come together in one workflow without needing separate design skills.

slides.heading: Working With Brand Kits
bullets: Save a client's logo, fonts, and colors once
Apply them to any template in one click
Keeps every piece of content looking consistently on-brand
slides.narration: Canva's Brand Kit feature lets you save a client's logo, brand colors, and fonts once, then apply them to any template with a click - this is how you keep every single piece of visual content looking consistently on-brand.

slides.heading: Resizing Content for Every Platform
bullets: One design, multiple platform sizes
Canva's Magic Resize handles most of it
Always double-check text doesn't get cut off
slides.narration: Canva can automatically resize one design into the different dimensions each platform needs, though it's good practice to double-check that text and logos aren't cropped after resizing, especially on smaller formats like Instagram Stories.

slides.heading: Building a Simple Template Library
bullets: Save your best-performing designs as templates
Duplicate and swap text/photos for new posts
Saves hours once you have a library built
slides.narration: As you work with a client, save your best-performing designs as reusable templates - for future posts, you just duplicate and swap the text and photo, turning a 20-minute design task into a 3-minute one.

lessons.title: AI Image Generation for Content (Midjourney, DALL-E)

slides.heading: AI Image Generation Basics
bullets: DALL-E and Midjourney turn text into original images
Great for concept visuals, blog headers, and social graphics
Always check a client's comfort level and usage rights
slides.narration: Tools like DALL-E (built into ChatGPT) and Midjourney generate original images from a text description - useful for blog post headers, quick concept visuals, or social graphics. Always confirm a client is comfortable with AI-generated imagery before using it in anything customer-facing.

slides.heading: Writing Effective Image Prompts
bullets: Describe subject, style, mood, and composition
Reference a visual style the client likes
Generate several options and pick the strongest
slides.narration: A strong image prompt describes the subject, the visual style, the mood, and the composition - referencing a visual style the client already likes helps a lot, and it's normal to generate several options before picking the strongest one.

slides.heading: Editing and Refining Generated Images
bullets: Rarely is the first result perfect
Ask for specific changes rather than a full regeneration
Combine with Canva for final text and branding
slides.narration: The first generated image is rarely perfect - ask for specific, targeted changes rather than regenerating from scratch each time, and plan to bring the final image into Canva to add text, branding, and any final polish.

slides.heading: Being Transparent About AI-Generated Images
bullets: Some audiences and platforms have disclosure norms
When in doubt, ask the client their preference
Honesty here protects both you and the client
slides.narration: Some audiences and platforms have real expectations around disclosing AI-generated imagery - when in doubt, ask the client their preference directly, since being upfront about this protects both of your reputations.

lessons.title: Grammarly and AI Editing Tools for Final Polish

slides.heading: Why a Final Editing Pass Still Matters
bullets: AI drafts can have subtle grammar or tone issues
A second AI-aware editing tool catches what you might miss
This is the layer that makes content feel truly polished
slides.narration: Even a strong AI-drafted piece can have subtle grammar issues or tone inconsistencies - running it through a dedicated editing tool like Grammarly catches what a quick read-through might miss, and this final pass is often what separates polished content from merely acceptable content.

slides.heading: Using Grammarly's Tone Detector
bullets: Flags when writing reads as too formal, harsh, or unclear
Useful cross-check against your brand voice profile
Doesn't replace your own judgment, but supports it
slides.narration: Grammarly's tone detector flags when a piece of writing reads as unexpectedly formal, harsh, or unclear - a useful cross-check against the brand voice profile you built for that client, though it should support your judgment, not replace it.

slides.heading: Plagiarism and Originality Checks
bullets: Run important published content through a checker
AI can occasionally echo common phrasing too closely
Especially important for SEO-focused blog content
slides.narration: For important published content, especially SEO-focused blog posts, it's good practice to run it through a plagiarism checker - AI models can occasionally echo commonly-used phrasing closely enough to matter for original, ranking-focused content.

slides.heading: Building Your Personal Editing Checklist
bullets: Tone matches the brand voice profile
No generic AI-sounding phrases slipped through
Facts, names, and numbers are verified
slides.narration: Build a simple personal checklist for every final piece: does the tone match the brand voice profile, have any generic AI-sounding phrases slipped through, and have every fact, name, and number been verified - running this same checklist every time builds real consistency.

modules.title: Module 3: Core AI Content Creation Skills

lessons.title: Writing High-Converting Social Media Captions with AI

slides.heading: The Anatomy of a Strong AI-Assisted Caption
bullets: A hook in the first line
The message or value in the middle
A clear call-to-action at the end
slides.narration: A strong caption usually has three parts: a hook in the very first line that stops the scroll, the actual message or value in the middle, and a clear call-to-action at the end - ask AI to draft with this structure explicitly in mind.

slides.heading: Prompting for Platform-Specific Captions
bullets: Instagram/Facebook: short-to-medium works well
TikTok: keep it very short, video does the talking
LinkedIn: more professional, value-driven tone
slides.narration: Always specify the exact platform in your prompt - Instagram and Facebook captions can be short to medium, TikTok captions should stay very short since the video carries most of the message, and LinkedIn calls for a more professional, value-driven tone.

slides.heading: Generating Variations and Picking the Best
bullets: Ask for 3-5 different hooks for the same post
Compare which one best fits the brand voice
Combine the best elements of different versions
slides.narration: Ask AI for three to five different hook options for the same post rather than accepting the first one, compare which best fits the brand voice profile you built, and don't hesitate to combine the strongest elements from different versions into one final caption.

slides.heading: Avoiding the Most Common AI Caption Tells
bullets: Overuse of certain words like 'elevate' or 'unlock'
Excessive emoji or exclamation points
Generic hooks that could apply to any business
slides.narration: Watch for common AI caption tells: overused words like "elevate" or "unlock," excessive emoji or exclamation points, and generic hooks so vague they could apply to literally any business - editing these out is what makes a caption feel genuinely written for this specific brand.

lessons.title: Blog Posts and SEO Content with AI Assistance

slides.heading: Starting With a Real Keyword or Topic
bullets: Research what the target audience actually searches
Give AI the specific keyword to write around
A vague topic produces vague, unfocused content
slides.narration: Before drafting anything, research what the target audience actually searches for, and give AI that specific keyword or topic to write around directly - a vague starting topic reliably produces vague, unfocused content.

slides.heading: Structuring an SEO-Friendly Blog Post
bullets: Clear headings that mirror how people search
A strong introduction that states the value upfront
A natural, non-repetitive use of the target keyword
slides.narration: Structure posts with clear headings that mirror how people actually search, a strong opening that states the value upfront, and a natural use of the target keyword throughout - never awkwardly repeated just to hit a count.

slides.heading: Fact-Checking AI-Generated Blog Content
bullets: AI can state outdated or incorrect information confidently
Verify every specific claim, statistic, or fact
Especially important in fast-changing industries
slides.narration: AI can state outdated or simply incorrect information with complete confidence - verify every specific claim, statistic, or fact independently before publishing, which matters even more in fast-changing industries where information ages quickly.

slides.heading: Adding a Genuinely Human Element
bullets: AI is weak at real client-specific stories or examples
Add a real client testimonial, case, or insider detail
This is often what actually makes content rank and convert
slides.narration: AI genuinely struggles to invent believable, specific client stories or insider details - adding one real testimonial, case study, or insider insight to an AI-drafted post is often exactly what makes it both rank better and convert better.

lessons.title: Email Newsletters and Sales Copy with AI

slides.heading: Structuring an Effective Newsletter
bullets: A subject line that earns the open
One clear main message, not five competing ones
A single, obvious call-to-action
slides.narration: An effective newsletter starts with a subject line that genuinely earns the open, focuses on one clear main message rather than five competing ones, and ends with a single, obvious call-to-action rather than several confusing options.

slides.heading: Writing Subject Lines That Get Opened
bullets: Curiosity, specificity, or a clear benefit work best
Avoid spam-trigger words and excessive punctuation
Test 2-3 options when the platform allows it
slides.narration: Strong subject lines lean on curiosity, specificity, or a clear stated benefit - avoid spam-trigger words and excessive punctuation or capital letters, and when the email platform supports it, test two or three subject line options.

slides.heading: Writing Sales Copy That Doesn't Feel Pushy
bullets: Lead with the customer's problem, not the product
Be specific about the actual benefit, not vague hype
End with one clear, low-pressure next step
slides.narration: Strong sales copy leads with the customer's actual problem rather than the product itself, describes specific real benefits rather than vague hype language, and ends with one clear, low-pressure next step rather than aggressive urgency.

slides.heading: Personalizing AI-Drafted Email Copy
bullets: Feed in real customer questions or feedback
Reference specific past purchases or behavior where relevant
Generic email copy gets ignored fast
slides.narration: Feed real customer questions, feedback, or specific past purchase behavior into your prompts wherever relevant - generic, one-size-fits-all email copy is easy for a reader to ignore, while specific, relevant copy earns real attention.

lessons.title: Editing AI Drafts Until They Sound Human (and On-Brand)

slides.heading: The Editing Pass That Actually Matters Most
bullets: A first draft is a starting point, not a final answer
Real editing is where the brand voice actually appears
Budget real time for this, don't rush it
slides.narration: Treat every AI first draft as a genuine starting point rather than a finished answer - the real editing pass, where you steer the tone back toward the client's specific brand voice, is where most of your actual value shows up, so budget real time for it.

slides.heading: Reading Everything Out Loud
bullets: Awkward AI phrasing is easier to hear than see
Reading aloud catches unnatural rhythm quickly
A fast, simple habit with a big quality payoff
slides.narration: Reading a finished piece out loud is one of the fastest ways to catch awkward AI phrasing or unnatural rhythm - it's a simple habit that consistently produces a noticeably higher-quality final result.

slides.heading: Cutting Generic Filler Language
bullets: Watch for vague phrases that say very little
Replace generic claims with specific, concrete details
Specificity is what makes content feel genuinely written
slides.narration: Watch for vague filler phrases that technically say something but communicate very little, and replace generic claims with specific, concrete details wherever possible - specificity is consistently what separates content that feels genuinely written from content that feels auto-generated.

slides.heading: Getting a Second Set of Eyes When Possible
bullets: Even experienced editors miss their own patterns
A quick peer review catches what you can't see
Not always possible, but valuable when it is
slides.narration: Even experienced editors develop blind spots to their own recurring patterns - a quick second read from a colleague or peer, when it's possible, reliably catches issues that are genuinely hard to see in your own work.

modules.title: Module 4: Building Your AI Content Portfolio

lessons.title: Creating Mock Content Campaigns

slides.heading: Why You Need Samples Before Your First Client
bullets: Clients want to see proof, not just a resume
A mock campaign shows your actual editing process
You control the quality with no deadline pressure
slides.narration: Since you may not have a paying client yet, building a mock content campaign for a fictional or real local business lets you show proof of your skills, not just claim them on a resume - and you control the quality with no deadline pressure.

slides.heading: Picking a Practice Business
bullets: Choose an industry you understand well
A real local shop works great (with permission)
Or invent a believable fictional brand
slides.narration: Pick an industry you already understand - maybe a coffee shop, a boutique, or a local service business. You can build a sample around a real business you admire (with their knowledge) or a believable fictional brand you invent yourself.

slides.heading: Building a Realistic Content Set
bullets: A week of social captions, plus one blog post and one email
Mix content types to show real range
Write COMPLETE finished pieces, not just topic ideas
slides.narration: Build a realistic content set: a week of social captions, one full blog post, and one email newsletter - mixing content types shows real range, and writing COMPLETE, finished pieces rather than rough topic ideas is what actually impresses a future client.

slides.heading: Documenting Your Editing Process
bullets: Show a raw AI draft next to your final edited version
Explain what you changed and why
This is what proves your actual editing skill
slides.narration: Show a raw AI first draft side by side with your final, edited version, and briefly explain what you changed and why - this before/after comparison is exactly what proves your real editing skill, not just your ability to write a prompt.

lessons.title: Building an AI Content VA Portfolio

slides.heading: What an AI Content Portfolio Needs
bullets: A short intro about you and your specialty
2-3 sample projects showing range and editing skill
Your process, not just the pretty finished pieces
slides.narration: A strong content portfolio has a short introduction about who you are and what you specialize in, two or three sample projects that show both range and editing skill, and a brief explanation of your process - clients want to understand HOW you think, not just see finished writing.

slides.heading: Where to Host Your Portfolio
bullets: A simple free website (Canva, Carrd, or similar)
A well-organized Google Drive folder works too
Keep the link short and easy to share
slides.narration: You don't need a paid website - a simple site built for free in Canva or Carrd, or even a neatly organized, view-only Google Drive folder, works perfectly well as long as the link is short and easy to share in a proposal or message.

slides.heading: Presenting Before/After AI Editing as Proof
bullets: Show the raw AI draft and your finished version
This proves editing skill, not just prompting ability
A powerful, easy-to-understand demonstration
slides.narration: Showing a raw AI draft next to your polished, finished version is one of the most powerful things you can put in a content portfolio - it immediately proves real editing skill in a way that's easy for any client to understand at a glance.

slides.heading: Keeping Your Portfolio Updated
bullets: Swap in real client work as soon as you have it
Remove your weakest samples over time
Revisit it every few months
slides.narration: As soon as you land real client work (with their permission to showcase it), swap it in for your mock samples, and keep quietly removing your weakest pieces over time so your portfolio only ever shows your current best work.

lessons.title: Showcasing Before/After Content and Engagement Results

slides.heading: Why Results Convert Better Than Promises
bullets: Numbers build trust faster than claims
Clients hire outcomes, not just good writing
Even small wins are worth showing
slides.narration: A specific number - even a modest one, like "30% more comments in six weeks" - builds trust faster than a vague promise about being a great writer, because it shows you deliver real outcomes, not just polished sentences.

slides.heading: What to Track From Day One With a New Client
bullets: Screenshot starting engagement numbers
Note the date you started managing their content
Repeat the same screenshot monthly
slides.narration: From the very first day with a new client, screenshot their starting engagement numbers, note the exact date you began, and repeat that same screenshot every month - this makes an honest before/after comparison easy to produce later.

slides.heading: Turning Numbers Into a Simple Case Study
bullets: One paragraph: the challenge
One paragraph: what you did
One paragraph: the result, with a number
slides.narration: A simple case study is just three short paragraphs: what challenge the client had, what you actually did about it, and what result followed - ideally with a real number attached to that last part.

slides.heading: Getting Permission to Share Results Publicly
bullets: Always ask before using a client's name or numbers
Some clients prefer to stay anonymous - that's fine
A quick written 'yes' protects you both
slides.narration: Always ask a client's permission before sharing their name, page, or specific numbers publicly - some are happy to be named, others prefer anonymity, and either way a quick written yes over email or chat protects you both.

modules.title: Module 5: Resume and Job Application Mastery for Content VAs

lessons.title: Writing an AI Content VA Resume

slides.heading: What Belongs on an AI Content VA Resume
bullets: A clear headline naming your specialty
Tools you know - ChatGPT, Jasper, Canva AI, etc.
A link to your portfolio, front and center
slides.narration: Your resume should open with a clear headline naming your specialty - "AI Content & Copywriting VA" - list the specific tools you know like ChatGPT and Canva AI, and put your portfolio link somewhere it can't be missed.

slides.heading: Describing Experience Without a Job History
bullets: Frame your training and mock projects as real work
Use action verbs - drafted, edited, launched
Quantify wherever you can, even mock numbers
slides.narration: If you don't have paid experience yet, describe your training and mock campaigns using strong action verbs - drafted, edited, launched, optimized - and quantify what you can, like "drafted and edited a 7-day content calendar across three platforms."

slides.heading: Formatting for Readability
bullets: Keep it to one page
Use short bullet points, not paragraphs
Consistent, clean font and spacing
slides.narration: Keep your resume to a single page with short, scannable bullet points rather than dense paragraphs, using a clean, consistent font - a client reviewing dozens of applicants will spend only seconds per resume.

slides.heading: Common Resume Mistakes to Avoid
bullets: Vague phrases like 'content expert'
No portfolio link at all
Typos - always proofread out loud
slides.narration: Avoid vague self-descriptions like "content expert" with nothing to back it up, never submit a resume without your portfolio link, and always proofread out loud before sending - typos undercut your credibility instantly in a writing-focused role.

lessons.title: Crafting Winning Proposals for Content Gigs

slides.heading: What a Good Proposal Includes
bullets: A quick read on their current content and voice
Your specific plan for improving it
Clear pricing and next steps
slides.narration: A strong proposal briefly summarizes what you noticed about their current content and brand voice, lays out your specific plan for improving it, and ends with clear pricing and an easy next step, like a short call.

slides.heading: Personalizing Every Proposal
bullets: Reference their actual content and recent posts
Never send an obviously copy-pasted pitch
Mention one specific opportunity you spotted
slides.narration: Every proposal should reference the client's actual content and something specific you noticed - an inconsistent tone, an untapped format, or an opportunity you spotted - a generic copy-pasted pitch is easy to spot and easy to ignore.

slides.heading: Structuring Your Pricing
bullets: Package by deliverables - posts, blogs, emails per month
Offer 2-3 clear tiers, not endless options
Be upfront about what's NOT included
slides.narration: Package your pricing around clear deliverables - a certain number of posts, blog articles, or emails per month - and offer two or three simple tiers rather than overwhelming a client with options. Be upfront about what falls outside the package too.

slides.heading: Following Up Without Being Pushy
bullets: One polite follow-up after about a week
Add new value, don't just 'check in'
Know when to move on gracefully
slides.narration: If you don't hear back, one polite follow-up after about a week is reasonable - ideally adding something new, like a quick content idea for their page, rather than just "checking in." If there's still no response after that, it's fine to move on gracefully.

lessons.title: Where to Find AI Content & Copywriting Clients

slides.heading: Freelance Platforms
bullets: Upwork, Onlinejobs.ph, and similar sites
Filter for content, copywriting, or 'AI writing' roles
A strong profile and portfolio link matter most
slides.narration: Freelance platforms like Upwork and Onlinejobs.ph list content and copywriting roles regularly, including a growing number specifically mentioning AI-assisted writing - filter for those, and make sure your profile headline and portfolio link are strong.

slides.heading: Local Small Businesses
bullets: Coffee shops, salons, gyms, boutiques nearby
Many have inconsistent or outdated content
A polite, specific outreach message works well
slides.narration: Local small businesses are often sitting on inconsistent or outdated content simply because the owner is busy running the business - a polite, specific outreach message pointing out one thing you could improve for them works well.

slides.heading: Referrals and Word of Mouth
bullets: Your first client is your best source of the next
Ask happy clients if they know anyone else
A short testimonial makes referrals even easier
slides.narration: Once you land one happy client, ask directly whether they know any other business owners who could use similar help - referrals convert far more easily than cold outreach, especially if you have a short testimonial to share.

slides.heading: Content and Marketing Communities
bullets: Facebook groups for content creators and marketers
Often share leads and job postings directly
Be an active, helpful member, not just a lurker
slides.narration: Facebook groups built around content creation and small business marketing often have owners posting that they need writing help, and dedicated communities frequently share leads too - being an active, genuinely helpful member tends to bring in the best opportunities.

lessons.title: Nailing the Discovery Call (Understanding Their Voice and Goals)

slides.heading: What Clients Are Actually Evaluating
bullets: Can you understand their brand quickly?
Do you ask smart, specific questions?
Will your writing genuinely sound like them?
slides.narration: In a discovery call, clients aren't just checking your writing samples - they're watching whether you can understand their brand quickly, whether you ask smart and specific questions about their voice, and whether they can imagine your writing genuinely sounding like them.

slides.heading: Questions You Should Ask Them
bullets: What does success look like to you?
What's frustrated you about content so far?
Show me one piece you loved and one you didn't
slides.narration: Come prepared with your own questions: what does success actually look like to them, what's frustrated them about content so far, and ask them to show you one piece they loved and one they didn't - this shows you're thinking like a real partner.

slides.heading: Talking About Pricing Confidently
bullets: Know your rate before the call, don't improvise
Explain what's included, not just the number
It's okay to say you'll follow up in writing
slides.narration: Decide your rate before the call so you're never improvising under pressure, explain clearly what's included for that price, and it's completely fine to say you'll send the full proposal in writing afterward rather than negotiating on the spot.

slides.heading: Following Up After the Call
bullets: Send a written summary within 24 hours
Restate what you understood about their voice and needs
Attach your proposal or next steps clearly
slides.narration: Within 24 hours of the call, send a short written summary restating what you understood about their voice and needs, attached to your proposal or a clear next step - this reinforces that you listened closely and keeps momentum going.

modules.title: Module 6: Landing Your First Content Client and Beyond

lessons.title: Onboarding a New Content Client

slides.heading: What Onboarding Actually Covers
bullets: Gathering their brand voice and past content
Getting access to the right accounts/tools safely
Agreeing on the first month's content plan
slides.narration: Onboarding is the process of getting properly set up with a new client: gathering their brand voice guidance and past content examples, gaining safe access to whatever accounts or tools are involved, and agreeing together on what the first month will actually look like.

slides.heading: Building Their Brand Voice Profile Together
bullets: Walk through the questions from Module 1 together
Collect real example content they've loved
Save it somewhere you'll actually reference it
slides.narration: Walk through the brand voice questions from Module 1 together on your first call, collect real example content they've genuinely loved, and save the resulting profile somewhere you'll actually reference every time you write for them.

slides.heading: Collecting Brand Assets and Guidelines
bullets: Logo files, brand colors, and fonts
Any existing brand guidelines document
Access to past-performing content, if available
slides.narration: Request the client's logo files, brand colors and fonts, any brand guidelines document they have, and access to their past-performing content if available - having these upfront saves a lot of back-and-forth later.

slides.heading: Setting the First 30 Days' Plan
bullets: Agree on content volume and platforms
Set your first check-in date
Clarify how and when you'll be paid
slides.narration: Before writing anything, agree on how much content you'll produce and on which platforms, set a date for your first check-in call, and make sure payment terms - amount, method, and schedule - are clearly agreed on both sides.

lessons.title: Pricing Your AI-Assisted Content Services

slides.heading: Why Clear Expectations Prevent Problems
bullets: Most client conflicts come from unspoken assumptions
A short written agreement protects you both
Revisit and adjust as the relationship grows
slides.narration: Most conflicts between a Content VA and a client come from things that were never actually agreed on out loud - a short written agreement covering scope, pricing, and response times protects you both and can always be revisited as things grow.

slides.heading: Common Pricing Models
bullets: Monthly retainer - most common for ongoing content
Per-piece - for one-off blog posts or campaigns
Package pricing - bundling multiple content types
slides.narration: A monthly retainer is the most common model for ongoing content work, a per-piece rate suits one-off blog posts or standalone campaigns, and package pricing that bundles several content types together is popular for clients wanting full-service support.

slides.heading: What to Include in Your Scope of Work
bullets: Number of pieces/platforms included per month
What counts as a 'revision' vs a new request
What's explicitly NOT included (e.g. paid ad copy)
slides.narration: Your scope of work should spell out exactly how many pieces and which platforms are included per month, what counts as a normal revision versus a brand-new request, and what's explicitly NOT included, like paid ad copywriting, unless you charge separately for that.

slides.heading: Raising Your Rates Over Time
bullets: Review rates as your skill and results grow
Give existing clients advance notice
New clients can start at your current rate
slides.narration: As your skills and track record grow, it's normal and healthy to raise your rates - give existing clients advance notice (30-60 days is common), while any brand-new client simply starts at your current, updated rate.

lessons.title: Managing Multiple Clients' Content Calendars

slides.heading: Staying Organized Across Clients
bullets: One shared calendar tool, separate client views
Color-code or label content by client
A weekly planning block prevents last-minute chaos
slides.narration: Managing several clients well usually comes down to using one content calendar tool for everyone, color-coding or labeling content clearly by client, and setting aside a dedicated weekly block to plan ahead rather than reacting day to day.

slides.heading: Avoiding Voice Mix-Ups Between Clients
bullets: Double-check which brand voice profile you're using
Never reuse a caption meant for another client
Build a simple pre-publish checklist
slides.narration: Writing in the wrong brand voice is a real and embarrassing risk once you're juggling multiple clients - always double-check which brand voice profile you're using before drafting, never copy-paste content written for one client into another's queue, and consider a short pre-publish checklist.

slides.heading: Batching Work for Efficiency
bullets: Draft a week's content for one client in one sitting
Batch AI prompting separately from editing
Batch client communications too
slides.narration: Batching similar tasks - drafting a whole week of content for one client in one sitting, doing all your AI prompting in one block and editing in another, or replying to all client messages at set times - is far more efficient than constantly switching between different types of work.

slides.heading: Knowing When You've Reached Capacity
bullets: Quality should never quietly slip as you add clients
Track your actual hours per client honestly
It's okay to pause new clients or raise rates instead
slides.narration: Watch for signs that quality is slipping as you take on more clients - rushed edits, missed brand voice details, slower replies. Track your real hours per client honestly, and remember it's completely fine to pause taking new clients, or raise your rates instead of stretching yourself too thin.

lessons.title: Handling Feedback and Revisions on AI-Assisted Content

slides.heading: Receiving Feedback Without Getting Defensive
bullets: Feedback is about the work, not you personally
Ask clarifying questions before revising
Thank the client for being specific
slides.narration: It's easy to feel personally criticized when a client pushes back on a piece of writing, but feedback is about the work, not you - ask clarifying questions if something's vague, and genuinely thank clients who give specific, actionable feedback.

slides.heading: Handling 'This Doesn't Sound Like Us' Feedback
bullets: One of the most common AI content complaints
Ask for a specific example that DOES sound right
Update your brand voice profile so it doesn't happen again
slides.narration: "This doesn't sound like us" is one of the most common pieces of feedback in this niche - ask for a specific past example that does sound right to them, and update your saved brand voice profile so future drafts improve rather than repeating the same miss.

slides.heading: Managing Scope Creep in Revisions
bullets: Define how many revision rounds are included
A brand-new content type isn't a 'revision'
Politely price extra requests separately
slides.narration: Define upfront how many rounds of revision are included per piece - a request for a completely new content type or campaign, rather than a tweak to the current one, isn't really a "revision," and it's fair to politely price that as an additional request.

slides.heading: Turning Difficult Clients Into Long-Term Ones
bullets: Most 'difficult' clients just want to feel heard
Consistent, calm communication builds trust
Know when a client truly isn't the right fit
slides.narration: Many clients who seem difficult at first just want to feel heard and kept in the loop - consistent, calm communication usually turns them into your most loyal clients over time. Occasionally, a client genuinely isn't the right fit, and it's okay to part ways professionally.

lessons.title: Growing Your AI Content VA Career

slides.heading: Leveling Up Your Skill Set
bullets: Go deeper into SEO and content strategy
Learn basic paid ad copywriting
Study analytics to know what content actually performs
slides.narration: As you grow, going deeper into SEO and overall content strategy, learning basic paid ad copywriting, and studying analytics more closely to know exactly what content actually performs all let you charge more and take on bigger, more strategic clients.

slides.heading: Deciding Between More Clients or Higher Rates
bullets: More clients means more income but more hours
Higher rates mean the same hours, more income
Most successful Content VAs eventually favor the second
slides.narration: At some point you'll choose between taking on more clients at your current rate, or fewer clients at a higher rate - most experienced Content VAs eventually favor raising rates over endlessly adding more clients, since it protects both quality and your own time.

slides.heading: Building Toward an Agency or Specialty
bullets: Some Content VAs eventually build a small team
Others stay solo and specialize deeply in one format
Both paths are valid - choose what fits your goals
slides.narration: Some experienced Content VAs eventually build a small team, subcontracting design or extra writing to other freelancers; others prefer staying solo and specializing deeply in one high-value format like email or SEO. Neither path is more "correct" - it depends on what kind of work-life you actually want.

slides.heading: Congratulations on Finishing This Training
bullets: You've covered the full AI Content VA skillset
You have a portfolio, resume, and pricing plan
Time to start applying with confidence
slides.narration: Congratulations - you've now covered the full AI Content & Copywriting VA skillset, from AI writing tools and brand voice to editing, portfolio-building, client acquisition, and long-term growth. You're ready to start applying and pitching with real confidence.
